title: Strictly Monotone Mapping is Monotone
theorem_text: A mapping that is strictly monotone is a monotone mapping.
proof_text:
If $\phi$ is strictly monotone, then it is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing.
If $\phi$ is strictly increasing, then by Strictly Increasing Mapping is Increasing, $\phi$ is increasing.
If $\phi$ is strictly decreasing, then by Strictly Decreasing Mapping is Decreasing, $\phi$ is decreasing.
Thus $\phi$ is monotone by definition.
review_reason: Each strict direction implies its corresponding weak direction, exhausting the alternatives in the definition of monotonicity.

title: Order Embedding into Image is Isomorphism
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets.
Let $S'$ be the image of a mapping $\phi: \struct {S, \preceq_1} \to \struct {T, \preceq_2}$.
Then:
$\phi$ is an order embedding from $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ into $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$
if and only if:
$\phi$ is an order isomorphism from $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ into $\struct {S', \preceq_2 \restriction_{S'} }$.
proof_text:
Let $\phi$ be an order embedding from $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ into $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$.
Then $\phi$ is an injection into $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ by definition.
From Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection, a mapping from a set to the image of that mapping is a surjection.
Thus the surjective restriction of $\phi$ onto $S'$ is an order embedding which is also a surjection.
Hence the result from Order Isomorphism is Surjective Order Embedding.
review_reason: Corestriction supplies surjectivity and preserves and reflects exactly the same order comparisons. Conversely an isomorphism onto the image therefore has both order properties in the ambient codomain.

title: Finite Totally Ordered Set is Well-Ordered
theorem_text: Every finite totally ordered set is well-ordered.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a finite totally ordered set.
From Condition for Well-Foundedness, $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is well-founded if and only if there is no infinite sequence $\sequence {a_n}$ of elements of $S$ such that $\forall n \in \N: a_{n + 1} \prec a_n$.
If it were the case that $\struct {S, \preceq}$ had such an infinite sequence, then at least some of the terms would be repeated in that sequence.
So there would be, for example:
$s_i \preceq s_j \preceq s_k \preceq s_i$
and $\preceq$ would therefore not be transitive and so not a totally ordered set.
So $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is well-founded.
The result follows from the definition of well-ordered set.
review_reason: Repetition in a strictly descending chain contradicts irreflexivity of the strict order by transitivity. The displayed weak cycle does not show failure of transitivity as claimed.

title: Subset of Well-Ordered Set is Well-Ordered
theorem_text: Every non-empty subset of a well-ordered set is itself well-ordered.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a well-ordered set.
Let $T \subseteq S$.
Let $X \subseteq T$.
By Subset Relation is Transitive, $X \subseteq S$.
By the definition of a well-ordered set, $X$ has a smallest element.
It follows by definition that $T$ is well-ordered.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The smallest-element axiom applies only to nonempty subsets. X was taken as an arbitrary subset, and the proof explicitly asserts it has a smallest element even when X is empty.

title: Associative and Anticommutative
theorem_text:
Let $\circ$ be a binary operation on a set $S$.
Let $\circ$ be both associative and anticommutative.
Then:
$\forall x, y, z \in S: x \circ y \circ z = x \circ z$
proof_text:
Let $\circ$ be both associative and anticommutative.
Then from Associative Idempotent Anticommutative:
$\forall x, z \in S: x \circ z \circ x = x$
and $\circ$ is idempotent.
Consider $x \circ y \circ z \circ x \circ z$.
We have:
$$x \circ y \circ z \circ x \circ z = x \circ \left({y \circ z}\right) \circ x \circ z$$
$$= x \circ z$$
Also:
$$x \circ y \circ z \circ x \circ z = x \circ y \circ \left({z \circ x \circ z}\right)$$
$$= x \circ y \circ z$$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Applying the cited identity xyx=x first with middle element yz and then to zxz evaluates the same associative product as xz and xyz.

title: Constant Operation is Associative
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set.
Let $x \left[{c}\right] y = c$ be a constant operation on $S$.
Then $\left[{c}\right]$ is an associative operation:
$\forall x, y, z \in S: \left({x \left[{c}\right] y}\right) \left[{c}\right] z = x \left[{c}\right] \left({y \left[{c}\right] z}\right)$
proof_text:
$$\left({x \left[{c}\right] y}\right) \left[{c}\right] z = c \left[{c}\right] z$$
Definition of Constant Operation
$$= c$$
Definition of Constant Operation
$$x \left[{c}\right] \left({y \left[{c}\right] z}\right) = x \left[{c}\right] c$$
Definition of Constant Operation
$$= c$$
Definition of Constant Operation
review_reason: Both bracketings evaluate to the fixed element c regardless of the inputs.

title: Idempotent Magma Element forms Singleton Submagma
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma.
Let $x \in S$ be an idempotent element of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
Then  $\struct {\set x, \circ}$ is a submagma of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
proof_text:
By Singleton of Element is Subset:
$x \in S \iff \set x \subseteq S$
By the definition of idempotence:
$x \circ x = x \in \set x$
Thus $\set x$ is a subset of $S$ which is closed under $\circ$.
By the definition of submagma, the result follows.
review_reason: The only product of two elements of the singleton is x times x, which equals x by idempotence. This gives closure in the ambient magma.

title: Subset Product within Commutative Structure is Commutative
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma.
If $\circ$ is commutative, then the operation $\circ_\mathcal P$ induced on the power set of $S$ is also commutative.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma in which $\circ$ is commutative.
Let $X, Y \in \powerset S$.
Then:
$$X \circ_\mathcal P Y = \set {x \circ y: x \in X, y \in Y}$$
$$Y \circ_\mathcal P X = \set {y \circ x: x \in X, y \in Y}$$
from which it follows that $\circ_\mathcal P$ is commutative on $\powerset S$.
review_reason: Commutativity identifies the products of each ordered pair of factors in the two displayed sets, giving equality.

title: Subset of Subset Product
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma.
Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$.
Let $X, Y, Z \in \powerset S$.
Then:
$X \subseteq Y \implies \paren {X \circ Z} \subseteq \paren {Y \circ Z}$
$X \subseteq Y \implies \paren {Z \circ X} \subseteq \paren {Z \circ Y}$
where $X \circ Z$ etc. denotes subset product.
proof_text:
Let $x \in X, z \in Z$.
Then:
$x \circ z \in X \circ Z$ and $z \circ x \in Z \circ X$
Now:
$Y \circ Z = \set {y \circ z: y \in Y, z \in Z}$
$Z \circ Y = \set {z \circ y: y \in Y, z \in Z}$
But by the definition of a subset:
$x \in X \implies x \in Y$
Thus:
$x \circ z \in Y \circ Z$ and $z \circ x \in Z \circ Y$
and the result follows.
review_reason: Every representation of an element of either smaller product has a factor from X, which is also in Y. The same factors witness membership in the larger product.

title: Cancellable Element is Cancellable in Subset
theorem_text:
Let $\left ({S, \circ}\right)$ be an algebraic structure.
Let $\left ({T, \circ}\right) \subseteq \left ({S, \circ}\right)$.
Let $x \in T$ be cancellable in $S$.
Then $x$ is also cancellable in $T$.
proof_text:
Let $x \in T$ be cancellable in $S$.
Then by definition, $x \in T$ is left cancellable in $S$.
It follows from Left Cancellable Element is Left Cancellable in Subset that $x \in T$ is left cancellable in $T$.
Again by definition, $x \in T$ is right cancellable in $S$.
It follows from Right Cancellable Element is Right Cancellable in Subset that $x \in T$ is right cancellable in $T$.
Thus $x$ is also both left cancellable and right cancellable in $T$.
So by definition, $x$ is cancellable in $T$.
review_reason: The left and right cancellation implications each restrict from S to T because the operations agree there.

title: Subsemigroup Closure Test
theorem_text:
To show that an algebraic structure $\left({T, \circ}\right)$ is a subsemigroup of a semigroup $\struct {S, \circ}$, we need to show only that:
$(1): \quad T \subseteq S$
$(2): \quad \circ$ is a closed operation in $T$.
proof_text:
From Restriction of Associative Operation is Associative, if $\circ$ is associative on $\struct {S, \circ}$, then it will also be associative on $\struct {T, \circ}$.
Thus we do not need to check for associativity in $\struct {T, \circ}$, as that has been inherited from its extension $\struct {S, \circ}$.
So, once we have established that $T \subseteq S$, all we need to do is to check for $\circ$ to be a closed operation.
review_reason: Closure gives a binary operation on T and the associative law on triples in T follows by restriction of the law on S.

title: More than one Left Identity then no Right Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.
If $\struct {S, \circ}$ has more than one left identity, then it has no right identity.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure with more than one left identity.
Take any two of these, and call them $e_{L_1}$ and $e_{L_2}$, where $e_{L_1} \ne e_{L_2}$.
Suppose $\struct {S, \circ}$ has a right identity.
Call this right identity $e_R$.
Then, by the behaviour of $e_R$, $e_{L_1}$ and $e_{L_2}$:
$e_{L_1} = e_{L_1} \circ e_R = e_R$
$e_{L_2} = e_{L_2} \circ e_R = e_R$
So $e_{L_1} = e_R = e_{L_2}$, which contradicts the supposition that $e_{L_1}$ and $e_{L_2}$ are different.
Therefore, in an algebraic structure with more than one left identity, there can be no right identity.
review_reason: Multiplying each distinct left identity by the hypothetical right identity forces both to equal it.

title: Element under Left Operation is Right Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \leftarrow}$ be an algebraic structure in which the operation $\leftarrow$ is the left operation.
Then no matter what $S$ is, $\struct {S, \leftarrow}$ is a semigroup all of whose elements are right identities.
Thus it can be seen that any right identity in a semigroup is not necessarily unique.
proof_text:
From Left Operation is Associative, $\leftarrow$ is associative.
By the nature of the left operation, $\struct {S, \leftarrow}$ is closed:
$\forall x, y \in S: x \leftarrow y = x \in S$
whatever $S$ may be.
So $\struct {S, \leftarrow}$ is a semigroup.
From the definition of left operation:
$\forall x, y \in S: x \leftarrow y = x$
from which it is apparent that all elements of $S$ are right identities.
From More than one Right Identity then no Left Identity, it also follows that there is no left identity.
review_reason: The projection operation proves the main claim about right identities. The final invocation excluding a left identity requires at least two distinct elements. On a singleton the unique element is also a left identity.

title: Element under Right Operation is Left Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \rightarrow}$ be an algebraic structure in which the operation $\rightarrow$ is the right operation.
Then $\struct {S, \rightarrow}$ is a semigroup all of whose elements are left identities.
Thus it can be seen that any left identity in a semigroup is not necessarily unique.
proof_text:
From Right Operation is Associative, $\rightarrow$ is associative.
By the nature of the right operation, $\struct {S, \rightarrow}$ is closed:
$\forall x, y \in S: x \rightarrow y = y \in S$
whatever $S$ may be.
So $\struct {S, \rightarrow}$ is a semigroup.
From the definition of right operation:
$\forall x, y \in S: x \rightarrow y = y$
from which it is apparent that all elements of $S$ are left identities.
From More than one Left Identity then no Right Identity, it also follows that there is no right identity.
review_reason: All elements are indeed left identities, but the final claim that there is no right identity invokes a result requiring multiple distinct left identities. A singleton has a right identity.

title: Left and Right Identity are the Same
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.
Let $e_L \in S$ be a left identity, and $e_R \in S$ be a right identity.
Then:
$e_L = e_R$
that is, both the left identity and right identity are the same, and are therefore an identity $e$.
Furthermore, $e$ is the only left identity and right identity for $\circ$.
proof_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure such that:
$\exists e_L \in S: \forall x \in S: e_L \circ x = x$
$\exists e_R \in S: \forall x \in S: x \circ e_R = x$
Then $e_L = e_L \circ e_R = e_R$ by both the above, hence the result.
The uniqueness of the left and right identity is a direct result of Identity is Unique.
review_reason: The product of any left identity with any right identity equals each of them, so all such elements coincide and give a unique two-sided identity.

title: Identity of Monoid is Cancellable
theorem_text: The identity of a monoid is cancellable.
proof_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a monoid whose identity is $e$.
Let $x, y \in S$ such that $x \circ e = y \circ e$
Then, by the definition of the identity:
$x = x \circ e = y \circ e = y$
... thus $x = y$ and the result is proved.
review_reason: The displayed equation proves right cancellation directly. The same defining identity gives left cancellation immediately since e times x equals x for every x.

title: Identity is only Idempotent Cancellable Element
theorem_text:
Let $e_S$ is the identity of an algebraic structure $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Then $e_S$ is the only cancellable element of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ that is idempotent.
proof_text:
By Identity Element is Idempotent, $e_S$ is idempotent.
Let $x$ be a cancellable idempotent element of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
$$x \circ x = x$$
$x$ is idempotent
$$= x \circ e_S$$
Definition of Identity
So $x \circ x = x \circ e_S$.
But because $x$ is also by hypothesis cancellable, it follows that $x = e_S$.
review_reason: The identity itself cancels on both sides by definition and is idempotent. Left cancellation of x in xx=xe forces any other proposed cancellable idempotent to equal e.

title: Set of all Self-Maps is Monoid
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set.
Let $S^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to itself.
Let the operation $\circ$ represent composition of mappings.
Then the algebraic structure $\struct {S^S, \circ}$ is a monoid whose identity element is the identity mapping on $S$.
proof_text:
By Set of All Self-Maps is Semigroup, $\struct {S^S, \circ}$ is a semigroup.
By Identity Mapping is Left Identity and Identity Mapping is Right Identity the identity mapping on $S$ is the identity element of $\struct {S^S, \circ}$.
Since $\struct {S^S, \circ}$ is a semigroup with an identity element, it is a monoid by definition.
review_reason: The cited semigroup theorem supplies closure and associativity of composition, and the identity mapping acts on both sides.

title: Test for Submonoid
theorem_text:
To show that $\left({T, \circ}\right)$ is a submonoid of a monoid $\left({S, \circ}\right)$, we need to show that:
$(1): \quad T \subseteq S$
$(2): \quad \left({T, \circ}\right)$ is a magma (i.e. that it is closed)
$(3): \quad \left({T, \circ}\right)$ has an identity.
proof_text:
From Subsemigroup Closure Test, $(1)$ and $(2)$ are sufficient to show that $\left({T, \circ}\right)$ is a subsemigroup of $\left({S, \circ}\right)$.
Demonstrating the presence of an identity is then sufficient to show that it is a monoid.
review_reason: With the submonoid convention used here, closure and inherited associativity give a subsemigroup. Its own two-sided identity then makes it a monoid.

title: Identity of Cancellable Monoid is Identity of Submonoid
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid, all of whose elements are cancellable.
Let $\struct {T, \circ}$ be a submonoid of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
Then the identity of $\struct {T, \circ}$ is the same element as the identity of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
proof_text:
By Identity of Monoid is Unique:
: there is only one identity element of $\struct {S, \circ}$
and:
: there is only one identity element of $\struct {T, \circ}$.
Let $e_S$ be the identity of $\struct {S, \circ}$, and $e_T$ the identity of $\struct {T, \circ}$.
From Identity is only Idempotent Cancellable Element, $e_S$ is the only cancellable element of $\struct {S, \circ}$ which is idempotent.
But all elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$ are cancellable.
Thus $e_S$ is the only idempotent element of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
Again, all elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$ are cancellable.
Thus from Cancellable Element is Cancellable in Subset, all elements of $\struct {T, \circ}$ are cancellable.
Thus, $e_T$ is the only element of $\struct {T, \circ}$ which is idempotent.
Thus, as $e_T \in S$, we have $e_S \circ e_T = e_T = e_T \circ e_T$ and thus $e_S = e_T$.
review_reason: The ambient cancellable monoid has only one idempotent. The identity of the submonoid squares to itself under the restricted operation and hence must be that ambient idempotent.

title: Cancellable Elements of Monoid form Submonoid
theorem_text: The cancellable elements of a monoid $\struct {S, \circ}$ form a submonoid of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
proof_text:
Let $C$ be the set of cancellable elements of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
Obviously $C \subseteq S$.
From Cancellable Elements of Semigroup form Subsemigroup, $\struct {C, \circ}$ is a subsemigroup of $S$.
Let $e_S$ be the identity of $\struct {S, \circ}$.
From Identity of Monoid is Cancellable, $e_S$ is cancellable, therefore $e_S \in C$.
As $e_S$ is the identity of $S$, we have that:
$\forall x \in C: x \circ e_S = x = e_S \circ x$.
Thus $e_S$ is the identity of $\struct {C, \circ}$, which is therefore a monoid.
As $C \subseteq S$, the result follows.
review_reason: The cited semigroup result gives closure and associativity on the cancellable elements. The ambient identity belongs to the subset and still acts as a two-sided identity.

title: Structure Induced by Abelian Group Operation is Abelian Group
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group whose identity is $e$.
Let $S$ be a set.
Let $\struct {G^S, \oplus}$ be the structure on $G^S$ induced by $\circ$.
Then $\struct {G^S, \oplus}$ is an abelian group.
proof_text:
From Structure Induced by Group Operation is Group, $\struct {G^S, \oplus}$ is a group.
From Structure Induced by Commutative Operation is Commutative, so is the pointwise operation it induces on $G^S$.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The cited results give the pointwise function structure both the group axioms and commutativity.

title: Power Set with Union is Commutative Monoid
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set and let $\powerset S$ be its power set.
Then $\struct {\powerset S, \cup}$ is a commutative monoid whose identity is $\O$.
The only invertible element of this structure is $\O$.
Thus (except in the degenerate case $S = \O$) $\struct {\powerset S, \cup}$ cannot be a group.
proof_text:
From Power Set is Closed under Union:
$\forall A, B \in \powerset S: A \cup B \in \powerset S$
From Set System Closed under Union is Commutative Semigroup, $\struct {\powerset S, \cup}$ is a commutative semigroup.
From Identity of Power Set with Union, $\O$ acts as the identity of $\struct {\powerset S, \cup}$.
It remains to be shown that only $\O$ has an inverse:
For $T \subseteq S$ to have an inverse under $\cup$, we require $T^{-1} \cup T = \O$.
From this it follows that $T = \O = T^{-1}$.
The result follows by definition of commutative monoid.
review_reason: Union is an associative commutative operation on subsets with the empty set as identity. A union equaling the empty set forces both factors empty, excluding every other inverse.

title: Power Set with Intersection is Commutative Monoid
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set and let $\powerset S$ be its power set.
Then $\struct {\powerset S, \cap}$ is a commutative monoid whose identity is $S$.
The only invertible element of this structure is $S$.
Thus (except in the degenerate case $S = \O$) $\struct {\powerset S, \cap}$ cannot be a group.
proof_text:
From Power Set is Closed under Intersection:
$\forall A, B \in \powerset S: A \cap B \in \powerset S$
From Set System Closed under Intersection is Commutative Semigroup, $\struct {\powerset S, \cap}$ is a commutative semigroup.
From Identity of Power Set with Intersection, we have that $S$ acts as the identity.
It remains to be shown that only $S$ has an inverse:
For $T \subseteq S$ to have an inverse under $\cap$, we require $T^{-1} \cap T = S$.
From this it follows that $T = S = T^{-1}$.
The result follows by definition of commutative monoid.
review_reason: Intersection is associative and commutative with identity S. An intersection equal to S requires both subsets to contain all of S.

title: External Direct Product of Semigroups
theorem_text: The external direct product of two semigroups is itself a semigroup.
proof_text:
* From External Direct Product Closure, the external direct product of two closed algebraic structures is closed.
* From External Direct Product Associativity, the external direct product of two associative algebraic structures is associative.
The result follows.
review_reason: The coordinatewise product is closed and associative by the two cited product results, which are the semigroup requirements.

title: External Direct Product Inverses
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S \times T, \circ}$ be the external direct product of the two monoids $\struct {S, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {T, \circ_2}$.
Let:
$s^{-1}$ be an inverse of $s \in \struct {S, \circ_1}$
and:
$t^{-1}$ be an inverse of $t \in \struct {T, \circ_2}$.
Then $\tuple {s^{-1}, t^{-1} }$ is an inverse of $\tuple {s, t} \in \struct {S \times T, \circ}$.
proof_text:
Let:
$e_S$ be the identity for $\struct {S, \circ_1}$
and:
$e_T$ be the identity for $\struct {T, \circ_2}$.
Also let:
$s^{-1}$ be the inverse of $s \in \struct {S, \circ_1}$
and
$t^{-1}$ be the inverse of $t \in \struct {T, \circ_2}$.
Then:
$$\tuple {s, t} \circ \tuple {s^{-1}, t^{-1} } = \tuple {s \circ_1 s^{-1}, t \circ_2 t^{-1} }$$
$$= \tuple {e_S, e_T}$$
$$= \tuple {s^{-1} \circ_1 s, t^{-1} \circ_2 t}$$
$$= \tuple {s^{-1}, t^{-1} } \circ \tuple {s, t}$$
Thus the inverse of $\tuple {s, t}$ is $\tuple {s^{-1}, t^{-1} }$.
review_reason: Multiplication in either order gives the ordered pair of coordinate identities, the product monoid's identity.

title: Morphism Property Preserves Cancellability
theorem_text:
Let:
$\phi: \left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right) \to \left({T, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}\right)$
be a mapping from one algebraic structure:
$\left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right)$
to another:
$\left({T, *_1, *_2, \ldots, *_n}\right)$
Let $\circ_k$ have the morphism property under $\phi$ for some operation $\circ_k$ in $\left({S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}\right)$.
Then if an element $a \in S$ is either left cancellable or right cancellable under $\circ_k$, then $\phi \left({a}\right)$ is correspondingly left cancellable or right cancellable under $*_k$.
Thus, the morphism property is seen to preserve cancellability.
proof_text:
We need to demonstrate the following properties:
* If $a \in S$ has the property that:
$\forall x, y \in S: x \circ_k a = y \circ_k a \implies x = y$
then:
$\forall x, y \in S: \phi \left({x}\right) *_k \phi \left({a}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right) *_k \phi \left({a}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)$
* If $a \in S$ has the property that:
$\forall x, y \in S: a \circ_k x = a \circ_k y \implies x = y$
then:
$\forall x, y \in S: \phi \left({a}\right) *_k \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({a}\right) *_k \phi \left({y}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)$
* To show the first of the properties above:
$$\left({x \circ_k a = y \circ_k a \implies x = y}\right)$$
$$\implies \left({\phi \left({x \circ_k a}\right) = \phi \left({y \circ_k a}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)}\right)$$
Mappings are many-to-one by definition
$$\implies \left({\phi \left({x}\right) *_k \phi \left({a}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right) *_k \phi \left({a}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)}\right)$$
Morphism Property
and thus left cancellability is demonstrated.
* And the second is like it, namely this:
$$\left({a \circ_k x = a \circ_k y \implies x = y}\right)$$
$$\implies \left({\phi \left({a \circ_k x}\right) = \phi \left({a \circ_k y}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)}\right)$$
Mappings are many-to-one by definition
$$\implies \left({\phi \left({a}\right) *_k \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({a}\right) *_k \phi \left({y}\right) \implies \phi \left({x}\right) = \phi \left({y}\right)}\right)$$
Morphism Property
and thus right cancellability is demonstrated.
review_reason: Equality of homomorphic images of xa and ya does not imply equality of xa and ya, so cancellation cannot be transferred that way. For example, reducing integers modulo 6 sends cancellable 2 under integer multiplication to a noncancellable residue.

title: Restriction of Homomorphism to Image is Epimorphism
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a homomorphism.
Then a surjective restriction of $\phi$ can be produced by limiting the codomain of $\phi$ to its image $\operatorname{Im} \left({\phi}\right)$.
proof_text:
Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a homomorphism.
Let $\operatorname{Im} \left({\phi}\right) = T'$
By Morphism Property Preserves Closure, $T'$ is closed.
From Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection, $\phi \to \operatorname{Im} \left({\phi}\right)$ is a surjection.
Thus $\phi: S \to T$ is an epimorphism.
Therefore, by suitably restricting the codomain of a homomorphism, it is possible to regard it as an epimorphism.
review_reason: The image is closed, and corestricting to it gives a surjective homomorphism. The T in the penultimate line must denote the restricted target T' for that line to hold, as the preceding and concluding lines specify.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Semigroups
theorem_text:
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ and $\left({T, *}\right)$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \left({S, \circ}\right) \to \left({T, *}\right)$ be an epimorphism.
Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a semigroup.
Then $\left({T, *}\right)$ is also a semigroup.
proof_text:
As $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a semigroup, then by definition it is closed.
As $\phi$ is an epimorphism, it is by definition surjective.
That is:
$T = \phi \left[{S}\right]$
where $\phi \left[{S}\right]$ denotes the image of $S$ under $\phi$.
From Morphism Property Preserves Closure it follows that $\left({T, *}\right)$ is closed.
As $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a semigroup, then by definition $\circ$ is associative.
From Epimorphism Preserves Associativity, $*$ is therefore also associative.
So:
$\left({T, *}\right)$ is closed
and:
$*$ is associative.
Therefore, by definition, $\left({T, *}\right)$ is a semigroup.
review_reason: Surjectivity identifies the target with the closed image, and associativity descends by the cited associativity result for epimorphisms.

title: Homomorphism Preserves Subsemigroups
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be semigroups.
Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a homomorphism.
Let $S'$ be a subsemigroup of $S$.
Then $\phi \paren {S'}$ is a subsemigroup of $T$.
proof_text:
By Restriction of Homomorphism to Image is Epimorphism, $\phi$ is an epimorphism onto its image .
Then by Epimorphism Preserves Semigroups, it follows that the image of $S'$ is a semigroup.
The result follows.
review_reason: Restricting the homomorphism to the subsemigroup gives a surjection onto its image. The image inherits the semigroup law and is a subset of T.
